summary.text: Meiosis is a special type of cell division of germ cells in sexually reproducing organisms, and it produces the gametes: sperm or egg cells.
DNA replication is followed by two rounds of division, giving four cells that each have half the number of chromosomes of the original cell.
Because the number is halved, two gametes can fuse into a zygote with two copies of each chromosome, so each generation keeps the same number.

facts.label: What it makes
facts.value: Four cells, each with half the original chromosomes

facts.label: Human numbers
facts.value: Gametes carry 23 chromosomes; body cells carry 46

facts.label: Crossing over
facts.value: Maternal and paternal chromosomes swap genetic material, making new combinations

facts.label: Who does it
facts.value: Sexually reproducing animals, plants and fungi, but not bacteria

facts.label: Female animals
facts.value: One large ovum and three small polar bodies

items.prompt: Why must a cell halve its number of chromosomes when it makes eggs and sperm?

options.label: Eggs and sperm need less DNA to be able to move
So the fused cell keeps the same number as its parents
So each egg ends up identical to its parent cell
So one parent can contribute more than the other

items.explain: Halving the number lets two gametes fuse into a zygote with two copies of each chromosome, so successive generations keep the same chromosome number.

items.prompt: Two siblings share the same parents, yet they are genetically different from each other and from both parents. Which part of the cell division that made their eggs and sperm helps explain this?

options.label: Chromosomes are copied exactly, with no mixing at all
Every gamete gets only the mother's chromosomes
Each gamete gets a full, unchanged set of chromosomes
Chromosomes swap pieces, making new mixes of maternal and paternal code

items.explain: Because of recombination, a chromatid can hold a new combination of maternal and paternal information, giving offspring that are genetically distinct from either parent.

items.prompt: A biologist follows meiosis in a female animal and counts the four cells that result. What typically happens to them?

options.label: One becomes an ovum; three are discarded as polar bodies
All four grow into full-sized eggs of equal size
Two become eggs and the other two become sperm cells
All four cells fuse back together into one big cell

items.explain: In female animals, three of the four products are typically eliminated into polar bodies, and only one cell develops to produce an ovum.

items.prompt: A single-celled bacterium multiplies into two cells. Is meiosis how it does it?

options.label: Yes; all single-celled life uses meiosis
Yes, but only when the food runs low
No; it generally splits asexually by binary fission
No; it first fuses with a partner cell, then splits in four

items.explain: Meiosis does not occur in archaea or bacteria, which generally reproduce asexually by binary fission.

items.prompt: Two cells have just finished the first meiotic division. What happens in the second division?

options.label: Sister chromatids separate into different cells, without new DNA replication
The DNA is copied again, then the homologs separate
The cells fuse to form a zygote
Nothing; four cells already exist

items.explain: The cells go into a second division without another round of DNA replication, and sister chromatids are segregated into separate daughter cells, for four haploid cells in total.

items.prompt: When a mistake in meiosis leaves a cell with an abnormal number of chromosomes, what can it lead to?

options.label: Nothing, because chromosome number doesn't matter
Stronger offspring with extra genetic material
Miscarriage or developmental disabilities
Offspring identical to both parents

items.explain: Errors in meiosis that cause an abnormal number of chromosomes are the leading known cause of miscarriage and the most frequent genetic cause of developmental disabilities.
